paragraphs.text: Huakang Oolong is an oolong grown in [Taiwan](taiwan:where-it-is), the island off the coast of Fujian. The record names only the island. That says where the leaf grew and nothing more: not the mountain, the height, the cultivar or the style. Where a seller names a mountain or township, that is the fuller claim.

Oolong is the [partly oxidised tea](oolong:definition), standing between green tea and red. On the island most of it is lightly to moderately oxidised and rolled into balls, with [Qingxin oolong](taiwan-oolong:definition) the main cultivar and Jinxuan the other common one. The plants and the craft came with settlers from that coast. In the 1860s the Scottish merchant John Dodd, working with the Taipei merchant Li Chunsheng, sold the island's tea abroad as [Formosa Oolong](taiwan-oolong:history).

brewing.text: Ball-rolled Taiwan oolong takes hot water, about 90 to 100°C, a fairly generous amount of leaf and short steeps; the balls open slowly and give many infusions. Roasted Dong Ding takes water from about 95°C to a full boil. Aged oolong takes very hot water, in a pot that holds its heat, clay above all. Oriental Beauty is the exception and takes cooler water, about 80 to 95°C.

notice.text: In light high mountain tea: a sweet, floral cup, often creamy or buttery, with little bitterness and a long sweet aftertaste. In roasted Dong Ding: caramel, ripe fruit, nuts and a toasted aroma. In Baozhong: floral notes and a clear, bright liquor. In Oriental Beauty: ripe fruit and honey, with little bitterness.
